newsitem.title: USA: US cash crudes hold onto modest gains to end week.
newsitem.headline: US cash crudes hold onto modest gains to end week.

text.p: U.S. cash crude prices wound down Friday at the same price levels seen since midday, posting slightly firmer results on the back of options expiry plays and nervousness over delays in renewed Iraqi sales.
Cash traders said activity was steady for most of the session, but grade differentials stuck to steady ranges for both sweet and sour parcels.
July West Texas Intermediate/Cushing talked late at $18.90-19.00 a barrel, steady from late Thursday. July/August screen spreads favored the second month by roughly 20 cents.

Traders said July Exchange for Physicals (EFPs) lost steam Friday, moving from around a 20 cents premium to paper values earlier in the day to only a 10-12 cents edge late. August EFPs were talked at only a five cents premium.
July NYMEX futures actually settled at $18.84 a barrel, 14 cents stronger than Thursday.

Cash traders said rumors a large U.S. Gulf refiner bought four million barrels of Nigerian Bonny Light deflated EFP values. EFPs have remained strong ever since May NYMEX futures contracts saw an inordinately large amount of foreign crude delivered against paper expiration matches. Even more foreign crude -- mostly Bonny Light -- was delivered against the June NYMEX contract.

Now, traders said it appears much of the Bonny Light overhang has been absorbed by various refiners over the previous few weeks, easing fears of more foreign deliveries and the need for such lofty EFP level.
Light Louisiana Sweet/St. James folded the week at a 16-14 cents discount to the benchmark, steady from Thursday. Deals were recorded at both 14 and 15 cents below the marker.
Heavy Louisiana Sweet/Empire firmed 10 cents to talk at a 60-50 cents discount, with Midland pegged close to the last trade at WTI/Cushing -37 cents.
West Texas Sour/Midland moved out at a $1.55-50 discount, 10 cents stronger, with Eugene Island at $2.03-$1.97 under WTI cash, traders said.
WTI/Cushing Postings were volatile, tracking July/August spreads. First sales of the day came around a $1.92-93 plateau, but talk faded back to the $1.85 level later.
News in the market again centered on Iraq, and the possible implications from delays in resuming oil sales under the U.N. oil-for-food accord.

Even though Iraq last week gained U.N. approval for another $2.14 billion in sales, there will be no new contracts approved until at least the end of June. The delay is called "ordinary" by U.N. officials to allow time for revising a new aid distribution plan and receive subsequent pricing formula.

Still, many in the market believe that Iraqi President Saddam Hussein wants to delay any new oil sales until the food and medicine distribution part of the deal catches up to the oil for money sector.
Iraqi U.N. envoy Nizar Hamdoon denied that Baghdad wanted to delay the oil sales any longer than it must, but cautioned on how long it would take to devise an equitable distribution plan.
